claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar-colony microstructure.
Under room-temperature tensile loading, dislocations pile up at internal lamellar or colony boundaries.
Dislocation pile-ups at lamellar-colony boundaries cause local stress concentrations, brittleness, and limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
A thermal annealing treatment followed by controlled aging will promote solute segregation at interphase boundaries.
The proposed treatment will modify the chemistry and structure of the lamellar boundaries.
Segregated solute atoms will increase interfacial cohesion.
Segregated solute atoms will reduce the impedance of internal boundaries to dislocation motion.
Reduced boundary impedance will diminish dislocation pile-ups and their localized stress concentrations.
Diminishing pile-up-induced stress concentrations will mitigate early microcrack initiation and propagation.
The annealed and aged alloy will have a lower propensity for microcrack nucleation than the untreated alloy.
The annealed and aged alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated alloy.
The treatment will retain or increase the alloy's strength.
Improved interfacial bonding may increase strength by approximately 10–20% relative to the untreated alloy.
A treatment temperature below the melting point but sufficiently high for solute mobility, followed by moderate-temperature aging, is applicable.
The proposed response is expected under room-temperature tensile testing representative of service conditions.
The predicted 10–20% strength enhancement is based on analogous treatments in similar alloy systems.
The hypothesis may apply only to similar eutectic high-entropy alloys having dual-phase lamellar microstructures.

contradictions.description: The intervention is called a 'single-step' annealing process while also including a distinct controlled-aging stage and being described as annealing followed by aging.
